mappings.note: Content is NOT this chapter: the stem carries the banner 'HOW I TAUGHT MY GRANDMOTHER TO READ' and asks what the grandmother's reciting from memory reveals. None of this chapter's five C-2.2 LOs (all pot-maker specific) can apply, and the C-2.1 LOs are about craft heritage, so the citation stops at the competency C-2.2 (close reading, inferring from a literary text). Reported as misfiled.

Also foreign content -- an extract from 'How I Taught My Grandmother to Read' (the village wedding, the grandmother in tears) testing the speaker's perspective and tone. That is first-person-voice analysis, which is an LO in chapter 8622 but has no counterpart among 8623's LOs, so cited at C-2.2 competency level. Reported as misfiled.

The extract is Arenla's case for weaving over pot making, and the sub-questions ask why she wants Sentila to switch. That is the mother's expectation set against the daughter's passion -- LO-8. Not LO-6: the pounding and the bamboo cylinders are only the premise here, the question asked is about the choice of vocation, not the order of the stages.

Pure grammar drill: complete five sentences with noun clauses. LO-10 is the only outcome naming noun and relative clauses. Mapped to the grammar outcome and not to a literature outcome even though every sentence uses characters from the story.

Underline the main clause and circle the subordinate clause in three sentences from the text -- the subordinate clauses are relative clauses ('where the grey and red clay was found', 'who had suddenly found momentum', 'which not only catered...'). LO-10 again, not LO-6, despite the clay content: nothing is asked about the craft.
Complete five sentences with relative clauses (whose, where, which, who). Squarely LO-10's second half. Not C-2.2 generally, because the LO exists and names this exact structure.

'The tradition and history of the people did not belong to any individual' -- what does it symbolise. The answer is collective custodianship of a craft, i.e. the heritage and the community that holds it: LO-4. Not LO-3, which is about placing the text as a contemporary craft narrative among similar writing; this asks what the text preserves, not what kind of text it is.

The significance of the closing line 'A new pot maker was born' -- this IS the resolution of the mother-versus-daughter conflict, which is the second half of LO-8. Chosen over LO-9 because the question is about how the story ends, not about what perseverance contributed along the way.

Asks directly for the role of perseverance, elaborated with reference to Sentila -- the third named element of LO-9. Not LO-8: the obstacles listed include her mother's refusal, but the question is about the quality that carried her through, not the conflict itself.

Classify dao, kiln, spatula, basket / dough, bamboo, clay, hay / pounding, rotating, shaping into tools, raw materials and process. The 'Process' column is the sequence of stages, so LO-6. Not LO-7: the words are sorted by function, and nothing is asked about the imagery they create.

A composition task -- write a dialogue between Sentila and Arenla using the prompts 'I feel/felt ... because', 'When you said/did ... it made me feel ...'. This is writing in a narrative style from another's experience: C-1.2. Cited at competency level because curriculum 86 has NO learning outcomes under CG-1 at all (all 7 LOs sit under C-2.1/C-2.2), so composition work can only be cited at competency level. Not C-2.3, which is composing literary texts with literary devices; this is a feelings-dialogue exercise. DEFECT: stem also holds an advert line, 'Click Here to Buy book on Amazon'.

Four-step write-up about the student's own skills and passions, including turning a passion into a profession. Writing from one's own experience: C-1.2, at competency level because CG-1 carries no outcomes. Not C-1.3, which is for real-life formats (invitation, notice, slogan); this is a reflective personal essay.

Determiners: spot more in the text, then fill blanks. A grammar drill, but the chapter's only grammar outcome, LO-10, is restricted to noun and relative clauses, so determiners have no LO to sit under -- cited at C-2.2 competency level rather than forced into LO-10. Reported as a frame gap.

'Who is the main character' -- identification of the protagonist. None of the five C-2.2 LOs covers character identification (they cover stages, imagery, conflict, mentorship, clauses), so cited at competency level. Not LO-8: knowing Sentila is the protagonist is not tracing the conflict.

Sentila's HIDDEN passion is pot making -- hidden precisely because the family does not sanction it. That is the opening term of LO-8's conflict. Not LO-9, which needs observation/mentorship/perseverance rather than the existence of the desire.
She observes the expert potters KEENLY -- observation is the first of the three learning routes named in LO-9. Not LO-6: the question is about how she watched, not about what the stages are.
What she does with her deep desire: hides it. Concealment from the family is the conflict in LO-8 before it surfaces. Not LO-9, which concerns how the skill is acquired.

Why Arenla discourages her -- messy, exhausting work. The mother's stated grounds are the family-expectation side of LO-8. Not LO-6, although the grounds refer to the craft's labour: the question probes her motive.
Arenla feels pot making brings a tiny FINANCIAL reward -- her economic argument against her daughter's choice, i.e. LO-8. Not LO-6: return on labour is not a stage of the process.
Trekking long distances for CLAY -- sourcing the raw material is the first stage of the process, so LO-6. Not LO-8: no comparison with weaving is asked for here, only what is fetched.
What Arenla wanted her to learn instead: handloom weaving. The alternative the family presses on her -- LO-8.

How Arenla describes weaving: a profitable job. Her case for the alternative vocation, LO-8. Not C-2.1-LO-4: weaving's profitability is an argument inside the family, not a statement about craft heritage.
Weaving brings a handsome income -- the same family-expectation argument, LO-8.
Weaving is a clean job (against pot making's mess) -- Arenla's contrast, LO-8.

Traditional skills are highly RESPECTED in their culture -- a statement about the standing of craft in the community, which is LO-4. Not LO-8: this is the community's valuation, not the mother's objection.

The VILLAGE COUNCIL notices that Arenla is not teaching her daughter. The community holding the craft to account is LO-4's second clause. Not LO-8, which is the family axis; the council is the community axis.

Match pictures to Khurja, Jaipur blue, Bengal terracotta, Andretta, Karigari and Longpi black pottery -- six regional craft traditions from six states, all outside the text. C-2.1-LO-4 will not carry it, because LO-4 is about what THIS account preserves about ITS community. C-4.2 (richness of culture and heritage across regions and their connections) is the nearest competency; CG-4 has no learning outcomes in this curriculum, so competency level is the ceiling. Reported as a frame gap.

The live task at the end of the stem is to read a story about the value of handicrafts and art in English or one's own language and review it -- the model answer reviews Galsworthy's 'Quality'. That is exactly LO-3's second clause, relating the text to the wider body of writing about inherited skills. DEFECT: the stem opens with the whole of the previous question and its full model answer before the real prompt.

The Onula extract: she sees the clumsy attempt, diagnoses tension, offers to teach, then demonstrates. Mentorship, the second element of LO-9. Not LO-8: Onula is neither family expectation nor Sentila's own passion; she is the teacher who unlocks the skill.

Describe the process of pot making as the expert potters do it -- mixing, pounding, left hand in the lump, rotating, spatula, rhythm, firing. LO-6 verbatim. Not LO-7: the answer wants the sequence, not the sensory effect.

The council's warning to Mesoba: traditional skills symbolise the history of the people and experts are obliged to pass them on. Community custodianship, LO-4. Not LO-8, because the pressure described is the community's duty claim rather than the domestic argument.

How she felt after a YEAR of training without success -- shame, frustration, persistence under a harsh teacher. LO-9 covers perseverance and the part mentorship plays. Not LO-8: her mother appears here as teacher, not as opponent.

'Onula stood there for a long time as if trying to absorb a new phenomenon' -- the two indistinguishable rows of pots are the proof that observation, mentorship and perseverance worked. LO-9. Distinguished from the 'A new pot maker was born' item above, which I put at LO-8 as the formal resolution; this line is about the mentor registering the achievement.

Which statement about the village council is correct -- they summoned Sentila's father. The community enforcing transmission of the craft: LO-4. Not LO-8, because the council is not a family expectation.
The council's warning is GENTLE -- the manner in which the community presses its claim, still LO-4. Not C-2.2: nothing about form or style is at issue, only what the community did.
Traditional skills are the shared COMMUNITY HERITAGE -- the exact proposition LO-4 names. Not LO-3, which asks what kind of text this is.
Traditional skills do not belong to SINGLE PERSONS -- the same custodianship idea from the other side, LO-4.
It is Arenla's strict cultural DUTY to pass on her knowledge -- transmission as a community obligation, LO-4. Not LO-8: the duty is owed to the community, not to her daughter's wishes.
Mesoba is SUPPORTIVE of his daughter -- the split inside the family that drives LO-8's conflict and eventually its resolution. Not C-2.1-LO-4: his stance is personal, not the council's.

Summoned by the elders, Mesoba defends her potential and promises support -- the father taking his daughter's side against the mother's refusal, LO-8. Not LO-4 despite the council setting: what is tested is his reaction.

Who pressured Arenla: the council AND her husband. The combined pressure is what breaks the deadlock, i.e. how the text resolves the conflict, LO-8. Cited there rather than LO-4 because the answer hinges on the husband as much as the council.
Mastering the craft proved incredibly DIFFICULT -- the difficulty that makes perseverance necessary, LO-9. Not LO-6: no stage of the process is being recalled.

Which statement about the pot making process is correct -- pounding stubborn clay in bamboo. A stage of the process, LO-6, and the distractors (handloom, electric oven, city shops) are all process alternatives.
Clay is pounded inside BAMBOO cylinders -- the softening stage, LO-6. Not LO-7: the fact is asked for, not its sensory rendering.
The tool used to shape softened clay is the SPATULA -- implement belonging to the shaping stage, LO-6.

Shaping requires a specific RHYTHM -- a condition of the shaping stage, and LO-6 stresses why the order and manner matter to the craft. Not LO-7: rhythm here is technique, not imagery the reader is asked to analyse.

Under her mother's STRICT eyes she becomes very clumsy -- the text's point about how the quality of the mentoring shapes the learning, LO-9. Not LO-8: the mother is teaching here, having already given in.
She trains ONE YEAR without producing a proper pot -- the measure of her perseverance, LO-9. Not LO-6: the duration is not a stage.
The clay collapses into a MISSHAPEN LUMP -- her repeated failure, which is what perseverance has to survive, LO-9. Not LO-6, which is about how the craft succeeds when done in order.
She feels DISCOURAGED, frustrated and ashamed -- the low point that LO-9's perseverance strand turns on. Not LO-8: the shame is at her own failure, not at her family's opposition.
Onula is the TURNING POINT -- the arrival of the mentor, the second element of LO-9. Not LO-8: the mentor is outside the family conflict.
Onula's character is thoughtful and generous -- the disposition that makes her mentoring work, LO-9. Not C-2.2 generally, because LO-9 names mentorship explicitly.
Onula OBSERVES Sentila struggling wearily -- the mentor's observation preceding intervention, LO-9.
What Onula recognises: Sentila lacks CONFIDENCE, not tools, clay or strength. The mentor's correct diagnosis, LO-9. Not LO-6: the distractors are process items but the right answer is not.
Instead of criticising, Onula creates a CALM environment -- mentoring method, LO-9.
Onula gives gentle words of REASSURANCE -- mentoring method again, LO-9.

How Onula's teaching style differs from Arenla's -- a direct comparison of two mentors, the clearest LO-9 item in the set. DEFECT: the answer field ends with 'Downloaded from www.pdf.tube PAGE 338 CBSE CLASS 9 ENGLISH R1'.
Onula's support helps Sentila RELAX -- the effect of good mentoring, LO-9.
After Onula's help she shapes a BEAUTIFUL pot -- mentorship producing the breakthrough, LO-9. Not LO-6: the pot is the result, no stage is asked for.

Her ultimate test comes when her mother falls UNWELL -- the mother's absence is what forces the conflict to its resolution, so LO-8. Not LO-9: the test is structural to the plot, not a matter of how she learned.
